title: Itamaraty and Brazil in the World: However, Although

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *sin embargo* from A2 Unit 28, *aunque* from A2 Unit 28 and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1: they put a fact against another, or concede a point. Diplomacy and trade agreements are full of "agreed, but...". Here they work on Itamaraty and Brazil's present-day links, with dated facts.

sections.title: However, although, nevertheless
rows: El acuerdo se firmó en enero de 2026; sin embargo, solo su parte comercial se aplica desde mayo.
*sin embargo*: a contrast, with a comma after it
Aunque el puente ya se unió, faltan los accesos.
Brasil tiene muchas fronteras; no obstante, resolvió casi todas sus disputas por negociación.
Hay defensores del acuerdo; sin embargo, otros lo critican.

items.spanish: El palacio de Itamaraty es de Niemeyer; sin embargo, sus jardines son de Burle Marx.
items.english: The Itamaraty palace is by Niemeyer; however, its gardens are by Burle Marx.

items.spanish: Aunque Lula ganó en octubre de 2026, asumirá el cargo en enero de 2027.
items.english: Although Lula won in October 2026, he will take office in January 2027.

items.spanish: El corredor une dos países; no obstante, todavía no está terminado.
items.english: The corridor joins two countries; nevertheless, it is not yet finished.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* and *no obstante* usually start a new clause, with a comma after them. *Aunque* joins two clauses in one sentence; with a fact (*aunque llueve*) it takes the indicative. When you give a present-day fact, add the date: the situation can change.
